text: Mixed precision: fewer bits per number The problem. float32 uses 4 bytes per number; bfloat16 and float16 use 2.
label: core

section: 6. mixed precision: fewer bits per number
text: Half the bytes means half the memory traffic, and on GPUs with tensor cores the 16-bit matmuls also run several times faster.
label: core

section: 6. mixed precision: fewer bits per number
text: Automatic mixed precision (AMP) gets most of that without rewriting the model: inside torch.autocast(device_type, dtype=torch.bfloat16) , ops on autocast's lists (matmuls, linear layers, attention) run in 16 bits, precision-sensitive ops (softmax, normalisation, losses) stay in float32, and the parameters themselves stay float32. bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range (8 exponent bits) with fewer mantissa bits: no overflow, so no loss scaling needed.
label: core

section: 6. mixed precision: fewer bits per number
text: The usual choice on recent GPUs. float16 has more mantissa but a narrow range: small gradients underflow to zero, so it needs torch.amp.GradScaler , which multiplies the loss by a large factor before backward, divides gradients before the step, and skips steps whose gradients overflowed. scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda") # only for float16 with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16): _, loss = model(x, y) scaler.scale(loss).backward(); scaler.step(opt); scaler.update(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) What bfloat16 did on this machine This is the result that does not transfer Data-centre NVIDIA GPUs since the A100 have bfloat16 tensor cores; there, bfloat16 matmuls run many times faster than float32 ones and AMP is close to free speed.
label: core
